planting.note: Sow over a very lean, alkaline mineral mix amended with extra limestone grit to mimic the native Queretaro hillsides, and expect this famously slow grower to take close to a decade before it reaches flowering size.

directions: Lophophora diffusa forms a soft, pale blue-green to grayish button with shallow, indistinct ribs and tufts of white wool in the areoles instead of true spines, closely related to but distinct from the better-known Lophophora williamsii, which has deeper ribs and a different alkaloid profile. Small cream to pale yellow flowers open from the woolly crown in spring and summer on mature plants. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage in a limestone-rich substrate, and water sparingly, letting the mix dry completely between soakings since the plant stores most of what it needs in its thick taproot. Protect from any frost, as this species is restricted in the wild to warm, arid hills in Queretaro, Mexico, and has no cold tolerance.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow in a warm, humid propagator over a mineral cactus mix; keep conditions consistently warm year-round, since this species needs roughly a decade of uninterrupted growth before it is mature enough to begin forming its distinctive cephalium.

directions: Melocactus azureus is prized for its powdery blue-gray, strongly ribbed body, a color that sets it apart from the green-bodied Melocactus matanzanus already common in cultivation. Once mature, it stops widening and instead produces a cephalium, a woolly, bristle-studded crown at the stem apex, from which small pink flowers and later pink fruit emerge in succession for years afterward. Native to limestone outcrops in Bahia, Brazil, it wants intense sun, a fast-draining mineral substrate, and a strictly dry, warm winter rest. Overhead watering onto the cephalium should be avoided, as trapped moisture there can lead to rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors over a gritty, fast-draining mix; this Chihuahuan Desert native tolerates light winter freezes once established outdoors but still needs bone-dry soil through cold spells.

directions: Coryphantha macromeris is named for its unusually long, finger-like tubercles, which give each cylindrical stem a shaggy, almost sea-urchin silhouette quite different from the shorter-tubercled Coryphantha elephantidens already grown in collections. Stems cluster readily with age, spreading into loose mats across the desert pavement of its native range in Texas, New Mexico, and northern Mexico. Large rose-purple flowers open at the stem tips in late summer and fall, typically after seasonal rains, followed by small greenish fruit. Give it full sun and a mineral, low-organic soil, and withhold water almost entirely during winter dormancy.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Seed germinates readily in a warm mineral mix, but most growers instead root stem cuttings, which establish much faster than seedlings and quickly form the tree-like, sparsely branched shrub typical of mature plants.

directions: Austrocylindropuntia subulata is an unusually leafy cactus for the opuntioid tribe, pushing out long, fleshy, awl-shaped true leaves up to 4 inches long along its cylindrical young stems before they eventually shed, in addition to the formidable yellowish spines that persist for years. With age it builds into a sparsely branched, tree-like shrub reminiscent of a cholla, topped with showy red-orange flowers. Native to the Andean foothills of Peru, Ecuador, and Bolivia, it is traditionally planted as a living fence or hedge because cut sections root easily when simply set in dry soil. Grow in full sun with sharp drainage, and protect from hard frost, though it tolerates brief light freezes better than many tropical columnar cacti.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow over a very gritty, low-organic mix; this Argentine steppe native is unusually cold-tolerant for an opuntioid when kept bone-dry, but winter wet combined with cold is fatal, so plan for covered or indoor winter storage in damp climates.

directions: Tephrocactus articulatus produces chains of chalky blue-green, egg-shaped segments armed with broad, flattened, papery white spines that rustle in a breeze and give the plant its common name. It stays low and clumping rather than climbing or branching tall, slowly spreading into a loose mound across arid steppe terrain in its native Argentina. Small white to pale pink flowers appear at the segment tips in late spring. Give it full sun, maximum drainage, and a near-total dry rest in winter, since it is markedly more cold-tolerant than most Opuntia relatives as long as its roots stay dry.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Start seed indoors in a warm, humid propagator; young stems grow quickly once established and will need a sturdy stake, trellis, or fence line to lean on as they begin to scramble and sprawl.

directions: Acanthocereus tetragonus produces sprawling, three- to four-angled stems edged with stout, curved spines that catch on anything nearby, much like strands of barbed wire, and it readily climbs over shrubs or fences if given support. Large white, trumpet-shaped flowers open only at night in summer and close by mid-morning, followed by edible red fruit similar in texture to dragon fruit. It is native to coastal hammocks and scrub from Florida through the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central America, making it one of the few true cacti native to the southeastern United States. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil, and expect stems cut back by hard frost to resprout readily from the base in the warmer parts of its range.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow thinly over a very fine, mineral-dominant mix and keep the propagator warm and lightly humid; seedlings of this miniature species are tiny and slow for the first year or two but speed up once a taproot establishes.

directions: Turbinicarpus pseudomacrochele stays tiny and solitary for most of its life, a gray-green globe barely larger than a marble, decorated with long, thin, papery-textured central spines that twist and curl back against the body. Pale yellow flowers roughly an inch across open from the woolly crown in late winter and early spring, often before the plant has visibly grown at all that season. It is native to limestone slopes in San Luis Potosi, Mexico, where habitat disturbance and illegal collection have made wild populations vulnerable, so nursery-propagated seedlings are the responsible way to grow it. Keep it in full sun with sharp mineral drainage and water only sparingly, as its small size makes it easy to overwater in cultivation.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Sow over a gritty mineral mix in consistent warmth; plants branch and cluster from the base with age, so allow extra room around the original seedling for offsets to fill in over the following years.

directions: Thelocactus leucacanthus clusters into tight groups of ribbed, pale blue-green stems densely covered in stiff, bright golden-yellow spines, a solid-colored spine display that distinguishes it from the banded, bicolor spines of the related Thelocactus bicolor already grown here. Large glossy yellow flowers, each with a faint reddish throat, open from the crown of mature stems in spring and can nearly cover the plant in a good year. It is native to rocky, semi-arid hillsides in Hidalgo and Queretaro, Mexico. Grow in full sun with excellent drainage, and keep it dry through winter to encourage the heaviest spring bloom.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
